item.title: Tui Bua calls for equal recognition of all ethnic communities under Constitution
item.description: All ethnic communities living in Fiji should be equally recognised and protected under the constitution, with everyone who calls the country home acknowledged as part of one community. This was the submission made by the Paramount Chief of Bua, Na Gone Turaga na Tui Bua, Ratu Makutu Nagagavoka, during the public consultation on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Nabouwalu.
item.content:encoded:
All ethnic communities living in Fiji should be equally recognised and protected under the constitution, with everyone who calls the country home acknowledged as part of one community.

This was the submission made by the Paramount Chief of Bua, Na Gone Turaga na Tui Bua, Ratu Makutu Nagagavoka, during the public consultation on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Nabouwalu.

Ratu Makutu says provisions should be included in the Constitution to recognise the different ethnic communities living in Fiji and guarantee their place and security in the country.

He says descendants of the Indian community and other ethnic groups have made Fiji their home, following decisions made by previous generations, and there is no reason why they should not continue to be recognised.

Drawing from his personal experience, Ratu Makutu says he attended primary and secondary school where he developed an understanding of the Hindi language.

He says he also shares close friendships with Indo-Fijian men and women in the villages of Bua, with people from different backgrounds maintaining strong relationships over the years.

Ratu Makutu says these relationships go beyond friendship, as communities have shared many positive experiences, supported one another and learnt from each other.

However, he says developments in the country's leadership and national affairs are creating concerns among ethnic communities about their future and security in the place they call home.

He believes the different communities living across Fiji are not being adequately recognised, which is contributing to uncertainty and fear.

Ratu Makutu is calling for the Constitution to clearly recognise all communities as people who belong to Fiji, stressing that everyone living in the country should be treated as part of one community.

item.title: Drug importer Samuel Vaisevuraki jailed for 27.5 years for meth, cocaine, and MDMA operation
item.description: A Fiji-born man has been sentenced to 27.5 years in prison for his involvement in a large-scale methamphetamine, cocaine and MDMA operation in New Zealand. 47-year-old Samuel Vaisevuraki was sentenced in the High Court at Wellington after pleading guilty to importing, possessing for supply, offering to supply and supplying 65.756 kilograms of methamphetamine, 30 kilograms of cocaine and three kilo
item.content:encoded:
A Fiji-born man has been sentenced to 27.5 years in prison for his involvement in a large-scale methamphetamine, cocaine and MDMA operation in New Zealand.

47-year-old Samuel Vaisevuraki was sentenced in the High Court at Wellington after pleading guilty to importing, possessing for supply, offering to supply and supplying 65.756 kilograms of methamphetamine, 30 kilograms of cocaine and three kilograms of MDMA.

He also admitted conspiring to import up to 500 kilograms of methamphetamine, between 25 and 35 kilograms of cocaine and 20 kilograms of MDMA.

The sentence is believed to be the longest imposed for drug-related offending in the Wellington courts.

The court heard that over six months in 2023, Vaisevuraki worked with associates in New Zealand and overseas to import significant quantities of drugs through airports and by sea.

The drugs were transported from Canada, Fiji and South Africa, with some arriving on FedEx freight planes.

Airport staff involved in the operation allegedly collected packages while bypassing Customs and border controls, while other drugs were delivered by ocean-going vessels.

Vaisevuraki and his associates referred to the different routes as “doors”, describing them as open or closed depending on their availability.

He sold methamphetamine for $160,000 per kilogram and charged a 40 percent fee for managing drug imports into New Zealand.

His operation came to an abrupt halt after he was found carrying $16,000 in cash during a routine traffic stop.

The court also heard that Vaisevuraki had previously been jailed for seven years in 2021 for his involvement in large-scale drug importation and distribution.

He was released in March 2023 and ordered to complete a community-based drug rehabilitation programme.

However, while undertaking the programme, he re-established his drug operation using encrypted communication software.

His offending was considered more serious because it was committed while he was on parole.

After being recalled to prison, Vaisevuraki also attempted to bribe a prison officer by offering $25,000 in exchange for bringing a cellphone and a $100 Prezzy card into prison.

During sentencing, Justice Victoria Heine said Vaisevuraki had directed and organised drug buying and selling on a commercial scale, had substantial influence over his associates and expected significant financial gains.

The judge says these factors indicated that he had played a leading role in the operation.

item.title: Mother's loss and family responsibilities didn't stop Tavua District Secondary School Dux Bulivorovoro from achieving his goals
item.description: Losing his mother in 2022 was one of the hardest moments in his life, but 19-year-old Quisic Mawi Bulivorovoro says the experience taught him to become more independent and responsible while remaining focused on his education. Bulivorovoro was named the Dux of Tavua District Secondary School after achieving 333 out of 400 marks in his annual examination.
item.content:encoded:
Losing his mother in 2022 was one of the hardest moments in his life, but 19-year-old Quisic Mawi Bulivorovoro says the experience taught him to become more independent and responsible while remaining focused on his education.

Bulivorovoro was named the Dux of Tavua District Secondary School after achieving 333 out of 400 marks in his annual examination.

Speaking to fijivillage News, he says he had to balance his studies with household responsibilities following the loss of his mother.

Despite the challenges, Bulivorovoro says he remained determined to achieve his goals, with the support of his father and siblings.

He says he was excited to receive the Dux Award and had expected the achievement because of the sacrifices, hard work and determination he had put into his studies.

Bulivorovoro also expressed gratitude to God Almighty for giving him the knowledge, wisdom and talent throughout his educational journey.

item.title: Traditional forgiveness must not replace justice for domestic violence survivors – Kuruleca
item.description: Women and children who experience domestic violence must never be pressured to forgive their abusers in the name of family unity, culture or tradition, as their safety and right to justice must always come first. Permanent Secretary for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Selina Kuruleca is strongly opposing any proposal that would allow traditional iTaukei forgiveness ceremonies to re
item.content:encoded:
Women and children who experience domestic violence must never be pressured to forgive their abusers in the name of family unity, culture or tradition, as their safety and right to justice must always come first.

Permanent Secretary for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Selina Kuruleca is strongly opposing any proposal that would allow traditional iTaukei forgiveness ceremonies to replace legal action in domestic and family violence cases.

Kuruleca says women and children have suffered in silence for far too long, with some facing pressure from their families and communities to forgive those who have abused them.

She says traditional reconciliation is an important part of iTaukei culture, but it must never be used to shield offenders from legal consequences.

Kuruleca stresses that anyone who assaults their partner or abuses a child must be held accountable, even if a traditional reconciliation ceremony has taken place.

She says domestic violence is not simply a family disagreement that can be resolved through traditional ceremonies, but a serious matter that must be dealt with by the justice system when an offence has been committed.

The Permanent Secretary says survivors must never be forced or pressured to forgive their abusers simply to restore peace within their families or communities.

She stresses that forgiveness is a personal choice, while accountability is a legal responsibility.

Kuruleca says Fiji has committed to protecting women and children through the Domestic Violence Act 2009 and national action plans aimed at preventing violence.

She warns that allowing offenders to escape legal consequences through traditional forgiveness would undermine these efforts and weaken protections for survivors.

Kuruleca says any proposed changes to Fiji's justice system must strengthen the protection of women, children and vulnerable family members rather than create opportunities for offenders to avoid accountability.

She further says the Ministry will continue working with traditional leaders, religious organisations and communities to ensure cultural practices support survivors rather than silence them.

Kuruleca stresses that no cultural practice, family arrangement or proposal should place the interests of an offender above the safety, dignity and rights of a victim.
